The wet weight at birth is around 0.8 grams [Wwb = around 0.8 grams], a modest initial mass that places the neonates in a comparable range to those of the congeneric species Chalcides chalcides. This modest birth mass is likely linked to the energetic constraints of gestation, and the subsequent growth trajectory is steep, leading toward the maximum body mass observed in adults. The relatively small size at birth also suggests a high degree of maternal investment in post-parturition yolk reserves, which are critical during the first few weeks when foraging efficiency is low.

The ultimate wet weight of an adult Western rock skink has been recorded at 12.91 grams [Wwi = 12.91 grams], representing a considerable increase from the neonatal stage. This asymptotic mass is achieved through a period of sustained somatic growth that extends well into the second year of life. Interestingly, the transition to reproductive viability is not concurrent with the attainment of maximum body mass. Instead, sexual maturation is a distinct milestone that occurs well before growth has ceased entirely. For females, the time since birth at puberty is estimated at approximately 365 days since birth [tp = approximately 365 days since birth] when maintained at a stable thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This 365-day interval aligns with the completion of the first full annual cycle, after which the females are capable of initiating vitellogenesis and mating. This timing likely reflects the need to acquire sufficient body condition and nutrient stores to support a successful first gestation.

Reproductive output in the Western rock skink is characterized by relatively small litters paired with a low reproductive frequency. Detailed field observations indicate that each female produces one litter per season [F_R_i = one litter per season], a reproductive mode consistent with many temperate-zone skinks that face a narrow window of favorable thermal conditions for gestation and parturition. Within each breeding event, a female typically gives birth to eight young per litter [N_R_i = eight young per litter], resulting in a modest annual reproductive rate. This combination of a single seasonal event and a moderate litter size represents a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring survival over maximizing total fecundity. The extended gestation period, combined with the energetic cost of bearing eight well-developed young, likely constrains the ability of females to produce more than one litter annually under natural conditions.

In respirometry trials conducted at a low ambient temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption was recorded at 0.0031 ml O2/min [JOi = 0.0031 ml O2/min]. This relatively low metabolic rate is typical for reptiles of this size and reflects the profound effect of temperature on physiological processes. The 15 °C condition approximates the cooler end of the species' active thermal range, and at this temperature, the metabolic machinery operates at a suppressed level, influencing digestion rates, locomotor performance, and overall activity budgets. Comparing this cold-exposed metabolism to the rates at higher temperatures underscores the strong metabolic sensitivity of Trachylepis sulcata. Such data are critical for constructing predictive metabolic models for this small, heliothermic skink.
